verses.text: When Solomon had finished the building of Yahweh’s house, the king’s house, and all Solomon’s desire which he was pleased to do,
Yahweh appeared to Solomon the second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.

Yahweh said to him, “I have heard your prayer and your supplication, that you have made before me. I have made this house holy, which you have built, to put my name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there perpetually.

As for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, in integrity of heart, and in uprightness, to do according to all that I have commanded you, and will keep my statutes and my ordinances;
then I will establish the throne of your kingdom over Israel forever, as I promised to David your father, saying, ‘There shall not fail from you a man on the throne of Israel.’
But if you turn away from following me, you or your children, and not keep my commandments and my statutes which I have set before you, but go and serve other gods, and worship them;

then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and I will cast this house, which I have made holy for my name, out of my sight; and Israel will be a proverb and a byword among all peoples.
Though this house is so high, yet everyone who passes by it will be astonished and hiss; and they will say, ‘Why has Yahweh done this to this land, and to this house?’

and they will answer, ‘Because they abandoned Yahweh their God, who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold of other gods, and worshiped them, and served them. Therefore Yahweh has brought all this evil on them.’”
At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, Yahweh’s house and the king’s house
(now Hiram the king of Tyre had furnished Solomon with cedar trees and cypress trees, and with gold, according to all his desire), King Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.
Hiram came out of Tyre to see the cities which Solomon had given him; and they didn’t please him.
He said, “What cities are these which you have given me, my brother?” He called them the land of Cabul  to this day.
Hiram sent to the king one hundred twenty talents  of gold.
This is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised, to build Yahweh’s house, his own house, Millo, Jerusalem’s wall, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up, taken Gezer, burned it with fire, killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and given it for a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon’s wife.
Solomon built in the land Gezer, Beth Horon the lower,
Baalath, Tamar in the wilderness,

all the storage cities that Solomon had, the cities for his chariots, the cities for his horsemen, and that which Solomon desired to build for his pleasure in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
As for all the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the children of Israel;
their children who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel were not able utterly to destroy, of them Solomon raised a levy of bondservants to this day.
But of the children of Israel Solomon made no bondservants; but they were the men of war, his servants, his princes, his captains, and rulers of his chariots and of his horsemen.
These were the five hundred fifty chief officers who were over Solomon’s work, who ruled over the people who labored in the work.
But Pharaoh’s daughter came up out of David’s city to her house which Solomon had built for her. Then he built Millo.

Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar which he built to Yahweh three times per year, burning incense with them, on the altar that was before Yahweh. So he finished the house.
King Solomon made a fleet of ships in Ezion Geber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.
Hiram sent in the fleet his servants, sailors who had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon.
They came to Ophir, and fetched from there gold, four hundred and twenty talents,  and brought it to king Solomon.

footnotes.content: Solomon finishes what he set out to do—the temple, his own house, everything his heart desired. It's a moment of completion, but also vulnerability. Sometimes when we finish our own work, we stand waiting to hear from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord appears again, this time at the end of Solomon's labor. He doesn't show up during the rush or the ambition—He comes after, when the work is done and there's room to listen. How patient the Lord is with our pace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God speaks a strange and tender thing: He has set His name in this house forever, and His eyes and heart will be there perpetually. He doesn't dwell where we've built Him a room—He dwells among people who trust His name. The building matters only because the prayers do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Walk before Me like David did—in integrity of heart, in uprightness. The Lord's promises hinge on a word: if. Not earning, not paying, but walking. It's the posture of a heart turned toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will establish your throne forever. The same promise given to David is renewed to Solomon, stretched out in grace. Yet even as God speaks forever, He knows what Solomon will choose. His promises don't bind our freedom, and they don't change when we turn away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if you turn away. The Lord speaks plainly, without anger—He simply names the condition and the consequence. There's no threat here, only truth. He's showing Solomon the map of his own choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will cut off Israel from the land. It's the loneliest kind of judgment—not because God doesn't love, but because He does. A parent sometimes must let a child face the consequence of turning away. The Lord's love doesn't prevent Him from being honest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Everyone who passes will hiss and be astonished. The temple, so magnificent, will become a sign—not of God's power, but of what happens when a people abandon the One who gave it. Even beauty can become a witness against us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because they abandoned Yahweh their God who brought them out of Egypt. The answer to every ruin is always the same: we forgot where we came from, who saved us, who walked with us. The tragedy isn't what God did—it's what we chose to forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty years of building. What takes two decades to complete can take one moment to lose. Solomon finished both houses—Yahweh's and his own. Perhaps that's already the story in miniature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram supplied the finest materials—cedar and cypress and gold—and Solomon repaid him with twenty cities in Galilee. Trade between kings, favor for favor. Even at the height of his glory, Solomon operates in the world of exchange and obligation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram came to see the cities and they didn't please him. Sometimes what looks like a gift to one person looks like a burden to another. The land Solomon gave away didn't meet Hiram's expectation—a small word on how even great men's offerings can miss the mark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He called them the land of Cabul, a name that means 'displeasing' or 'like nothing.' Hiram's disappointment stuck to those cities forever. Sometimes our discontent leaves a mark deeper than we intend.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram sent one hundred twenty talents of gold. Yet after rejecting Solomon's cities, he still sends treasure. Perhaps even in disappointment, there's room for respect, even friendship between kings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This levy built the temple, the palace, Millo, Jerusalem's wall, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer—the whole architecture of Solomon's kingdom. Military strength, walls, storehouses. A magnificent construction, yet built on conscripted labor. Power often builds itself on the backs of those with no choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh took Gezer, burned it, killed the Canaanites in it, then gave it to his daughter as a wedding gift. An act of violence wrapped in tenderness. Solomon inherited a city purchased with blood and given as love—and he accepted it. Sometimes we inherit complications we don't examine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon built Gezer and Beth Horon the lower. Fortifications, strategic places. Each city is a move in the game of power and protection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baalath, Tamar in the wilderness. The names scatter across the map—a kingdom stretching far, each place a claim, a garrison, a reach into distance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the storage cities, cities for chariots and horsemen, all that Solomon desired to build for his pleasure. His pleasure. The kingdom exists partly for his vision, his desire, his building. It's not wrong, but it's visible—the king living out his dream on the canvas of a nation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the people left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites—the ones who remained in the land the Lord had given Israel. They were not destroyed; they remained, absorbed into Solomon's kingdom in a different kind of subjection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon raised them as a levy of bondservants to this day. The text says 'to this day'—as if the one who wrote this knew how the bondage would outlast Solomon. What looks like efficiency in a king's moment often carries a longer shadow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Of the children of Israel Solomon made no bondservants. The Lord's people were free to serve as warriors, officers, captains. There's a distinction here—one people bonded, the other honored. It works smoothly until it doesn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five hundred fifty chief officers overseeing the people who labored. An immense bureaucracy of oversight, management, control. Each one of them tasked with keeping the others working.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's daughter came up from David's city to her house, and Solomon built Millo. A foreign woman at the heart of Jerusalem, accommodated with buildings and honor. Solomon's marriages, like his cities, are part of his strategy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: Solomon brought burnt offerings and peace offerings to the Lord three times a year, maintaining the practice even as his kingdom expanded in every direction. We recognize the pattern—the rituals continue even when the heart drifts. It's easy to keep the calendar and forget the covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon made a fleet of ships at Ezion Geber, on the Red Sea—a new horizon, a reach toward trade and treasure. The sea was not his native calling; the temple was. But now his ambitions sail further out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram sent his sailors who knew the sea to serve Solomon's venture. Even the old king of Tyre, unsatisfied with Solomon's gift of cities, still sends his best people to help. There's a complexity in power—rivalry and respect often move together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They came to Ophir and fetched four hundred twenty talents of gold. A fortune brought back, more wealth poured into the treasury. Solomon's reach extends far, and his grasp is deep. But all the gold in the world never quite fills what it was meant to fill.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
